Deliverables.title: Data Import
Deliverables.description:
Supports structured Excel/CSV imports with validations, rollback, and post-processing logic to load high-volume data into core BART modules.

Video POC

Lucid Chart Tech Stack

Data Import Epic - Complete Multi-Phase Vision

Epic Overview

This epic delivers a high-throughput import pipeline that ingests large Excel (.xlsx/.xlsb) and CSV files and loads them into an in-memory staging table on our MS SQL database. Python workers will handle parsing/streaming, schema mapping, and type coercion with integrity safeguards to prevent data corruption, while heavy validation runs in the database to gate promotion of clean records into a master table. The flow supports deterministic batching, back-pressure, and clear error reporting; on validation failure it performs transactional rollback and writes to the audit log, leveraging the existing rollback capabilities in the current MS SQL environment. The POC scope is to prove fast, clean ingestion from Excel into the in-memory staging layer, verify .xlsb compatibility, and confirm end-to-end data fidelity and worker reliability. Completion means representative large files process without corruption, validations execute server-side, failures roll back safely with audit traceability, and only vetted data is committed to the master table; outputs include worker code, staging/master schemas, validation routines, and an audit-linked rollback playbook.
 
Phase 1: POC - Fast In-Memory Ingestion (Current State)

Scope
Prove that we can ingest large Excel/CSV files into SQL Server memory-optimized temp tables with blazing speed, zero data corruption, and full worker reliability.

What's Built in Phase 1 ✅

Fast Ingestion Pipeline:
Python workers (4 parallel) using Polars for 2-5x faster parsing vs pandas
Lambda pre-splitting: Excel files converted to CSV and split into chunks on S3
Workers download only their chunk (90% bandwidth reduction)
Memory-optimized temp tables: temp_import_{upload_id} with SCHEMA_ONLY durability
BULK INSERT with CSV intermediary for maximum throughput (4,000-8,000 rows/sec)

File Processing:
Direct S3 upload with presigned URLs
SQS message queue for worker coordination
Support for CSV, XLSX, XLSB formats
Multi-tab Excel detection and processing
Deterministic batching: Large files auto-split (e.g., 500K rows → 8 chunks)

Infrastructure:
4 Docker containerized workers with resource limits
LocalStack for local S3/SQS simulation
SQL Server 2022 with memory-optimized filegroup
Fan-out poller (mimics Lambda S3 trigger locally)

Performance & Reliability:
Comprehensive metrics collection (parse time, DB write time, throughput)
Worker health monitoring and graceful shutdown
SQS visibility timeout for automatic retry
Idempotency via file hash checking

Phase 1 POC Success Criteria ✅

✅ Representative large files (500K+ rows) process without corruption
✅ Excel (.xlsx, .xlsb) and CSV formats supported
✅ In-memory staging tables achieve target throughput (4K-8K rows/sec)
✅ Worker reliability confirmed (error handling, retry, metrics)
✅ End-to-end data fidelity maintained (no data loss or corruption)

What's NOT in Phase 1 ❌

❌ Schema mapping / column templates
❌ Database-side validation (temp tables have no constraints)
❌ Master table promotion workflow
❌ Rollback capabilities (no master tables to roll back yet)
❌ Audit logging (no import batches to track)
❌ Type coercion with integrity safeguards

Note: Some placeholder code for templates, staging tables, application-layer validation, and rollback stored procedures exists in the codebase but is NOT active in Phase 1. This code will be removed/replaced in future phases with proper database-side implementation. Rollback capabilities require master tables and batch tracking, which are future phase features.
 
Phase 2: Template System & Schema Mapping (Future)

Scope
Enable configurable templates for different import types with intelligent column mapping.

Features to Build

Template Management:
Admin-defined templates with column definitions
Data type specifications (string, integer, decimal, date, boolean)
SQL type mapping (NVARCHAR, INT, DECIMAL, DATETIME2, BIT)
Required field flags and default values
Column aliases for fuzzy matching

Schema Mapping:
Intelligent column mapping between file headers and template columns
Fuzzy matching with Levenshtein distance algorithm
Confidence scoring for suggested mappings
Save and reuse mappings for recurring imports
Manual override for low-confidence mappings

Database Schema:
templates - Template definitions
template_columns - Column specifications per template
template_column_aliases - Alternative column names for fuzzy matching
column_mappings - Saved mappings for reuse

Integration:
Workers detect template from upload metadata
Map file columns to template columns during ingestion
Store mapped data in standardized format
 
Phase 3: Database-Side Validation (Future)

Scope
Implement heavy validation in SQL Server to prevent corrupt data from entering master tables.

Features to Build

Validation Engine (Database-Side):
SQL Server stored procedures for validation logic
Triggers on staging tables for real-time validation
CHECK constraints for data type integrity
Foreign key validation where applicable
Custom validation routines (regex, ranges, business rules)

Validation Types:
Required Fields: NOT NULL constraints + validation checks
Type Coercion: CAST/CONVERT with TRY_CAST for safe type conversion
Range Validation: MIN/MAX checks for numeric/date fields
Pattern Matching: Regex validation for formatted fields (email, phone, etc.)
Referential Integrity: FK checks against lookup tables
Business Rules: Custom stored procedures for complex validation

Validation Storage:
staging_imports - Holds validated data with status flags
validation_status column: 'pending' → 'valid' / 'error' / 'warning'
validation_errors column: JSON array of specific errors per row
Indexed by upload_id, validation_status for fast filtering

Transactional Rollback:
Validation runs within database transaction
On validation failure: ROLLBACK transaction, data never enters staging
Write validation errors to audit log
Worker receives validation failure response and updates upload status

Architecture Change:
Remove application-layer validation in Node.js (temp code in template.server.ts)
All validation logic moves to SQL Server stored procedures
Validation executed as part of bulk insert transaction
Integrity safeguards prevent corruption at database level
 
Phase 4: Master Table Promotion & Approval Workflow (Future)

Scope
Gate promotion of validated data from staging to master tables with approval workflow.

Features to Build

Staging → Master Flow:
Data ingested into staging_imports (memory-optimized, no indexes)
Database validation runs (stored procedures/triggers)
Only rows with validation_status = 'valid' are eligible for approval
User reviews validation results via UI
On approval: sp_approve_and_import moves data to master table
Master table has full indexes, constraints, triggers

Import Batches:
import_batches table tracks each approval/import operation
Links staging records to master records via batch_id
Enables batch-level rollback (delete all rows for a batch)
Tracks status: 'pending' → 'importing' → 'completed' / 'rolled_back'

Master Table Architecture:
Dynamic master table creation per template (sp_create_master_table)
Full indexing for query performance
Foreign key to import_batches for rollback capability
Audit fields: imported_at, imported_by, batch_id

Approval UI:
Display validation statistics (total, valid, error, warning counts)
Paginated view of staging data with errors highlighted
Filter by validation status
Export validation errors to CSV
Approve button (only if valid_rows > 0)
 
Phase 5: Rollback & Audit Trail (Future)

Scope
Provide transactional rollback of imported batches with full audit traceability.

Features to Build

Rollback Mechanism:?
sp_rollback_batch stored procedure
Deletes all master table rows for a given batch_id
Updates import_batches.status = 'rolled_back'
Atomic transaction (all-or-nothing)
Preserves staging data for potential re-import

Audit Logging:
import_batches table serves as audit log
Tracks: upload_id, template_id, total_rows, imported_rows, status
User attribution: imported_by, rolled_back_by
Timestamps: imported_at, rolled_back_at
Optional rollback_reason field for documentation

Rollback UI:
Batch history view per upload
Rollback button with confirmation dialog
Reason input field for audit trail
Display rollback history with timestamps and users

Existing Capabilities Leveraged:
MS SQL Server transactional capabilities (BEGIN TRAN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK)
Foreign key cascade options (if needed)
Transaction log for point-in-time recovery (backup/restore)
 
Complete Architecture (All Phases)

Data Flow

1. Upload file to S3 (presigned URL)
2. Lambda converts Excel → CSV and splits into chunks
3. Worker downloads chunk from S3
4. Parse with Polars (fast, in-memory)
5. Map columns to template schema
6. Write CSV to shared volume
7. BULK INSERT into staging_imports (memory-optimized)
8. Database validation runs (stored procedures/triggers)
   - Valid rows: validation_status = 'valid'
   - Invalid rows: validation_status = 'error', validation_errors populated
9. User reviews validation results
10. User approves → sp_approve_and_import
11. Valid rows copied to master table with batch_id
12. Optional: Rollback batch via sp_rollback_batch

Database Schema (Complete)

Phase 1 (Current):
uploads - Upload metadata and status tracking
temp_import_{upload_id} - Fast ingestion temp tables (dynamic)
performance_metrics - Worker metrics and throughput data

Phase 2+ (Future):
templates - Template definitions
template_columns - Column specifications
template_column_aliases - Fuzzy matching aliases
column_mappings - Saved mappings
staging_imports - Validated staging data (memory-optimized)
import_batches - Batch tracking for rollback/audit
master_{template_name} - Master tables (one per template, dynamic)

Key Stored Procedures (Future)??

sp_validate_staging_data - Database-side validation logic
sp_approve_and_import - Promote staging → master
sp_rollback_batch - Atomic batch deletion with audit
sp_get_staging_data - Paginated staging data with stats
 Deliverables

Phase 1 (Delivered) ✅
✅ Python worker code with Polars processors (CSV, XLSX, XLSB)
✅ Memory-optimized temp table architecture
✅ Lambda pre-splitting optimization (Excel → CSV chunks)
✅ Performance metrics collection and reporting
✅ Worker reliability (error handling, retry, monitoring)
✅ End-to-end data fidelity validation
✅ Documentation (README, COMPLETE_DOCUMENTATION.md)

Phase 2+ (Future) 🔜
🔜 Template management system (database schema + API)
🔜 Fuzzy column mapping with confidence scoring
🔜 Database-side validation (stored procedures + triggers)
🔜 Staging table architecture with validation status tracking
🔜 Master table promotion workflow (sp_approve_and_import)
🔜 Rollback stored procedures with audit trail (sp_rollback_batch)
🔜 Approval UI with validation error display
🔜 Batch management UI with rollback capability
🔜 Comprehensive validation playbook (SQL validation patterns)
 
Production Readiness Roadmap

Phase 1 (Current):
LocalStack for S3/SQS
Fan-out poller (Node.js) mimics Lambda
Docker Compose with 4 workers

Future Phases - AWS Migration:
Replace LocalStack with AWS S3/SQS
Deploy Lambda for Excel→CSV conversion and chunking
Deploy workers to AWS Fargate with auto-scaling
Use RDS for SQL Server (with memory-optimized enabled)
CloudWatch monitoring for metrics and alerts
SNS notifications for import completion/failures

Future Phases - Scale Considerations:
Increase worker count based on load
Implement connection pooling for database
Add Redis cache for template/mapping lookups
Consider read replicas for master table queries
Implement queue prioritization for SLA requirements

Audit & Compliance Workflow
Deliverables.description:
Goal
Record an audit row inside the same transaction as each business write (source = RDS for SQL Server), then replicate those audit rows to a separate SQL Server “warehouse” for fast reads/search/exports—without loading the OLTP database.
Scope
ORM: Prisma (interactive transactions).
Source (authoritative): RDS for SQL Server; audit rows written by DB triggers into a local audit_events table (or your existing audit table).
Target (warehouse): Secondary SQL Server (RDS or EC2-hosted) receiving ongoing replication (AWS DMS).
Reads: Timeline/search APIs and large exports can read from the warehouse; small timelines may still read from source.
 High-Level Architecture

flowchart LR
  App[Node + Prisma] -->|$transaction| SrcDB[(RDS SQL Server - OLTP)]
  SrcDB -- AFTER triggers --> Audit[audit_events (same txn)]
  Audit -- AWS DMS (full load + CDC) --> Wh[(SQL Server Warehouse)]
  Wh --> APIs[Timeline/Search APIs & Exporter]
Atomicity: Triggers insert into audit_events in the same transaction as the business change.
Distribution: AWS DMS streams changes to the warehouse within seconds (eventual consistency for reads).
 Workstreams & Tasks
1) Event Contract & Taxonomy (unchanged)
Fields: event_id (GUID/ULID), occurred_at (UTC), tenant_id, user_id, action, entity_type, entity_id, status, payload_json (redacted), correlation_id.
Document allowed actions and entity naming; keep payload_json lean.
2) Source DB: Session Context + Triggers (centralized, atomic)
Per request/tx (Prisma): set session context once using sp_set_session_context for tenant_id, user_id, correlation_id before any writes in the transaction.
AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on audited tables:
Determine action, capture keys from INSERTED/DELETED.
Set occurred_at = SYSUTCDATETIME().
Read tenant_id, user_id, correlation_id via SESSION_CONTEXT().
Insert one row per affected row into [dbo].[audit_events].
Trigger hygiene: no network calls; set-based insert; skip the audit table to avoid recursion; keep payload/diff minimal.
If you already have an audit table, you can keep it and make it the replication source.
3) Source DB: Table & Indexes
audit_events columns = contract above; PK on event_id; clustered index on (tenant_id, occurred_at, event_id).
Nonclustered indexes for common reads:
(tenant_id, case_id, occurred_at, event_id) INCLUDE (action, status, user_id)
(tenant_id, user_id, occurred_at, event_id) INCLUDE (action, status)
(tenant_id, action, occurred_at, event_id) INCLUDE (status)
DB settings: READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON. Read-only login for read paths.
4) Replication: AWS DMS from Source → Warehouse
DMS replication instance in same VPC; security groups allow access to source RDS and target warehouse.
Endpoints: Source = RDS SQL Server; Target = SQL Server (RDS/EC2).
Task: Full load of audit_events → then ongoing replication (CDC) for changes.
Pre-reqs on source (high-level): appropriate permissions; recovery model and CDC settings per DMS guidance.
Mapping/Transforms: 1:1 schema; optional computed columns (e.g., day partition key) on target.
Monitoring: CloudWatch/DMS metrics for latency, errors; alarms on task stopped, latency > SLA (e.g., 60s).
5) Warehouse: Schema, Indexing & Analytics Layout
Mirror audit_events schema.
Add analytics indexes (and optionally partitioning by date or columnstore index if supported by your edition/needs).
Create views for common queries (case timeline, user activity, action counts) to keep APIs simple.
6) Read APIs & Exporter
Timeline/Search APIs:
Default to warehouse for interactive reads; strict tenant filter; keyset paginate by (occurred_at, event_id).
Fall back to source DB for freshest reads if replication lag > SLA.
Exports (SQS→Lambda→S3):
Prefer the warehouse for large ranges (reduces OLTP load).
Keep small admin exports against source if needed.
7) Data Quality & Reconciliation
Nightly rollup job compares row counts per tenant/day between source and warehouse; alert on drift.
Spot checks: min/max event_id/occurred_at per partition; mismatch raises an incident.
On DMS errors, follow replay runbook (restart from checkpoint).
8) Observability & Alarms
DMS: replication latency, full-load progress, errors → SNS/Chat + on-call.
Warehouse: CPU/IO, connection count, storage, slow queries.
Triggers: log and count failures (e.g., constraint errors) to a small audit_trigger_errors table; alarm if >0.
9) Security & Governance
TLS for DB connections; least-priv logins.
PII: ensure sensitive keys are redacted before they ever hit the audited columns.
Access control: separate read roles on the warehouse for APIs vs analysts.
10) Prisma Integration (minimal change)
Keep application writes unchanged; wrap business writes in $transaction.
At tx start, set SESSION_CONTEXT via tx.$executeRaw once.
No per-write audit code needed—the triggers do the work.
 Acceptance Criteria
Atomicity at source: Any committed business write produces exactly one row in audit_events; rollbacks remove it.
Replication SLA: The same row appears in the warehouse within ≤ 60 seconds under normal load.
Read correctness: Timeline/search APIs return ordered results (occurred_at, event_id) with strict tenant isolation.
Performance: Triggers add < 5–10% overhead on audited writes; OLTP stays healthy.
Observability: DMS lag/health, trigger errors, and warehouse slow queries are monitored with actionable alerts.
DQ parity: Daily source↔warehouse rollups match; discrepancies generate incidents.
 Notes & Options
Same-instance alternative: If the warehouse DB lives on the same SQL Server instance, triggers can write directly to [WarehouseDb].[dbo].[audit_events] in the same transaction (cross-database). For cross-instance, stick with DMS (recommended).
Ordering: Use occurred_at + event_id for total order; generate event_id via NEWID() in trigger or pass an app ULID through a column the trigger reads.
Fallback reads: If DMS is down or lagging, APIs can temporarily read from the source OLTP for small windows.
If you want, I can turn this into a task board (Terraform for DMS + SGs, minimal T-SQL trigger template, Prisma SESSION_CONTEXT helper, DQ job, and the alarm set).

Tasks.title: Create a Grid with the ability to export Excel Serverless with server pagination/sort
Tasks.description:
Goal
Users request an export; we generate it off the request path and return a pre-signed S3 URL. Source is RDS for SQL Server (existing audit table).
Scope
Formats: CSV now; PDF/DOCX optional.
Infra: S3, SQS (+ DLQ), Lambda (Node 20, VPC), Secrets Manager.
App: POST /exports to enqueue; GET /exports/{id} to fetch status + URL.
Happy-path flow

flowchart LR
  U[Client] -->|POST /exports| API
  API -->|insert PENDING| JOB[(export_jobs)]
  API -->|SQS msg {jobId, from, to, format}| Q[SQS]
  Q --> W[Lambda worker]
  W -->|stream MSSQL -> CSV| S3[(S3 exports)]
  W -->|row/byte counts, DONE| JOB
  U -->|GET /exports/{id}| API
  API -->|pre-signed URL| U
For huge windows: add a Chunker (split by day) and Finalizer (concat/zip/manifest) Lambdas. Same API.
Data model
export_jobs: job_id (ULID), tenant_id, params_json, format (csv|pdf|docx), status (PENDING|RUNNING|DONE|FAILED), s3_key, row_count, bytes_written, error_message, created_at, updated_at.
export_chunks (optional): job_id, chunk_index, from_ts, to_ts, status, s3_key, counts, attempts.
Message schema (SQS)

{"jobId": "01H...","tenantId": "t-123","from": "2025-09-01T00:00:00Z","to": "2025-09-30T23:59:59Z","format": "csv","chunkIndex": 0}
Worker (Lambda) — CSV
Open MSSQL (read-only login; READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled).
Streaming SELECT (indexed by tenant/scope/date) → CSV stringifier → S3 multipart upload (no buffering).
Write header row first; stable column order.
Update job (or chunk) with row_count, bytes_written, status.
Idempotency: key S3 parts by {jobId,chunkIndex}; safe to retry.
Timeouts: keep each chunk < 10–12 min; Lambda max is 15 min.
Concurrency: reserved concurrency 3–5 to protect the DB.
Optional formats
PDF: stream rows → PDFKit (page header repeat, fixed columns) → S3. For massive sets, split into volumes and zip/manifest. or Carbone for Crystal Reports
DOCX: summaries or small tables via docx library; for big data, prefer CSV (Excel row limit ~1,048,576).
API surface
POST /exports → validates filters (caps date range), inserts export_jobs, enqueues SQS, returns { jobId }. Also writes an audit row for the export request.
GET /exports/{jobId} → returns { status, url? } with pre-signed URL (TTL ≤ 1h) when DONE.
Guardrails
Date range cap: e.g., ≤ 31 days for CSV; stricter for PDF/DOCX.
Concurrency limits: per-tenant limit (e.g., 2) + global cap via Lambda reserved concurrency.
Indexes: covering on (tenant_id, <scope>, occurred_at, event_id) with INCLUDE columns frequently selected.
Security: S3 SSE-KMS, block public access, least-priv IAM; Secrets Manager for DB creds.
Observability & alarms
Dashboards: SQS backlog/age, DLQ depth, worker duration/error rate, rows/bytes per job, DB CPU/IO & connections.
Alarms: DLQ > 0, backlog age high, worker error rate > 1%, DB connections > 80%.
Performance targets (rule-of-thumb)
Per worker: ~3–12 MB/s MSSQL → S3.
100k rows (~20–200 MB depending on row width): ~10–45s.
Start with 3 workers → ~9–36 MB/s aggregate.
Acceptance criteria
Users can request and download CSV exports via pre-signed URL; API remains responsive.
Jobs/parts are ordered by (occurred_at, event_id) and include a header row.
Large windows complete via chunking; final artifact is one CSV or a zip/manifest.
DB remains healthy under parallel exports (no blocking, CPU/IO within budget).
Failures land in DLQ, alert on-call; replay runbook verified.

Supports structured Excel/CSV imports with validations, rollback, and post-processing logic to load high-volume data into core BART modules.
 
This epic delivers a high-throughput import pipeline that ingests large Excel (.xlsx/.xlsb) and CSV files and loads them into an in-memory staging table on our MS SQL database. Python workers will handle parsing/streaming, schema mapping, and type coercion with integrity safeguards to prevent data corruption, while heavy validation runs in the database to gate promotion of clean records into a master table. The flow supports deterministic batching, back-pressure, and clear error reporting; on validation failure it performs transactional rollback and writes to the audit log, leveraging the existing rollback capabilities in the current MS SQL environment. The POC scope is to prove fast, clean ingestion from Excel into the in-memory staging layer, verify .xlsb compatibility, and confirm end-to-end data fidelity and worker reliability. Completion means representative large files process without corruption, validations execute server-side, failures roll back safely with audit traceability, and only vetted data is committed to the master table; outputs include worker code, staging/master schemas, validation routines, and an audit-linked rollback playbook.

Tasks.title: Import POC Step 1 - Ensure that XLSX, XLSB and CSV multi-tabbed get imported to an in memory staging table
Tasks.assigneeId: Slava Bevza, Joshua Wakefield, Andros Haggins
Tasks.description:
Data Import – Multi-Format Worker Concept
Goal
 Extend our data import pipeline so workers can efficiently process large files in multiple formats (CSV, XLSX, XLSB, etc.) and push the data into a staging table in SQL Server.
High-Level Flow
Upload
User uploads a file (CSV/XLSX/XLSB) via the frontend.
File is stored in S3 (or equivalent) and an import record is created.
Dispatch
A job is queued with the file metadata (location, type, size).
One or more workers pick up the job.
Multi-Format Read
Based on file type, the worker uses an appropriate reader to:
Stream or load rows from CSV, XLSX, or XLSB.
Normalize columns to a consistent internal schema.
Chunking & Processing
Rows are processed in chunks (e.g., N rows per batch) to keep memory usage predictable.
Per-chunk transformations/validations are applied as needed.
Staging Insert
Each chunk is bulk-inserted into a SQL Server data staging table.
The system tracks progress per file (rows processed, batches completed).
Scaling
Multiple workers can run in parallel, each handling different files.
Design keeps workers stateless so we can scale horizontally (more containers = more throughput).
Key Requirements
Must support at least: CSV, XLSX, XLSB.
Must be able to handle large files (hundreds of MB / millions of rows) without blowing memory.
Insert into staging using batched/bulk operations for speed.
Expose clear logging/metrics so we can see throughput and bottlenecks.
Non-Goals (for now)
No complex business validation in this layer—focus is on fast, reliable ingestion into staging.
No tight coupling to a single library or vendor; implementation should be swappable as long as it meets the contract above.

Tasks.description:
The mapping process begins by selecting a target table—representing the database structure the import will ultimately write to—and creating a mapping template that aligns columns from an uploaded Excel sheet to the corresponding fields in that table. After the Excel file is uploaded, the system attempts exact column-name matches, with manual adjustments needed when names differ. Once the mapping is saved, it becomes a reusable template that can support multiple import jobs for the same case, enabling reimports or rollbacks without rebuilding the mapping each time. Each job loads data into a staging table, where it can then be validated, reviewed for errors, and corrected before committing to the master table. Throughout the workflow, progress updates often require manual refresh, and validation errors may relate to unmapped or mismatched fields. Overall, the mapping process cascades from the fixed import target schema → to the mapping template → to individual import jobs, each moving data through staging, validation, and final commit.

Mapping Workflow Summary
Start by selecting a target table
Represents the database table the import will eventually write to.
Structure (columns, data types, required fields) is fixed and cannot be changed in the app.
Create a new mapping for that target
Upload the Excel file to map.
Initial upload can take 2–3 minutes before the sheet becomes available.
System attempts automatic column matching
Performs exact name matching only.
Any mismatched names (e.g., “Claim Number” vs. “Claim”) must be mapped manually.
Save the mapping template
Becomes a reusable configuration for future imports for that case/table.
Useful when repeated imports or rollbacks are expected.
Create import jobs using the saved mapping
Each job pulls in the Excel sheet and places data into a staging table.
Defaults cascade from the mapping to each new job unless overridden.

Tasks.title: Data Import - Refine and clarify User Stories
Data Import POC Step 1 - Rust Excel to CSV Pre-Processor
Tasks.description:
Rust Excel to CSV Converter (Lambda Integration)

Goal: Replace slow JavaScript Excel reading (XLSX library) in Lambda fan-out with fast Rust converter. Keep all existing chunking, worker processing, and database logic unchanged.

Use /start.sh to run locally on docker. Uses Localstack to simulate AWS.

Rust → CSV → Chunks → Workers (existing)

Local Setup Note

The API server (including api.upload.fan-out.ts) runs on your local computer, not in Docker. Therefore:
Install Rust on your local computer (not in Docker)
Build the Rust binary on your local computer
Place binary at project root: ./excel-converter
The fan-out function will call it from your local computer
 
Architecture Flow

graph LR
    A[User Upload] --> B[Lambda Fan-Out]
    B --> C{File Type?}
    C -->|XLSX/XLSB| D[Rust Converter]
    C -->|CSV| E[Split CSV into Chunks]
    D -->|CSV| E
    E --> F[Upload Chunks to S3]
    F --> G[Workers Process Chunks]
    G --> H[Batch & Insert to SQL Server]
 
Detailed Flow

User Upload (XLSX/XLSB/CSV)
    ↓
Lambda fan-out receives file
    ↓
Check file extension (.xlsx, .xlsb, .csv)
    ↓
If XLSX/XLSB:
  → Download to /tmp/input.xlsb
  → Call Rust binary: /opt/bin/excel-converter --input /tmp/input.xlsb --output /tmp/output.csv
  → Rust reads Excel → writes CSV (fast, low memory)
  → Upload CSV to S3
    ↓
Split CSV into chunks
    ↓
Upload chunks to S3
    ↓
Workers download chunks (no changes to worker code)
    ↓
Existing Python worker logic (unchanged)
    ↓
Existing batched insertion to SQL Server (unchanged)
    ↓
Mark job complete
 
Key Points

Minimal change: Only Excel conversion in Lambda is replaced with Rust
No worker changes: Python workers continue processing CSV chunks (zero changes)
Same architecture: All existing chunking/queuing logic stays the same
DB safety: Your existing worker batching prevents database flooding
Low risk: Clear separation between conversion and processing
Lambda layer: Rust binary deployed as Lambda layer at /opt/bin/excel-converter
 
Developer Tasks

1. Build Rust Converter Binary
Create Rust CLI that reads XLSX/XLSB and outputs CSV
Use calamine crate for Excel reading
Accept --input and --output file path arguments
Return exit code 0 on success, 1 on error

2. Set Up Rust Locally (for local testing)
Install Rust on your local computer: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
Build the binary: cargo build --release
Copy to project root: cp target/release/excel-converter ./excel-converter
Test it works: ./excel-converter --help

3. Update Fan-Out Code
Replace XLSX library call with Rust binary in convertExcelToCSV() function
Use ./excel-converter locally, /opt/bin/excel-converter in production
Add /tmp file handling and cleanup
Keep all existing chunking logic unchanged

4. Test & Validate
Unit test: Rust converter with sample XLSX file
Unit test: Rust converter with sample XLSB file (122MB Kroll file)
Integration test: Full Lambda flow with XLSX upload
Integration test: CSV upload (ensure no regression)
Benchmark: Time Rust conversion vs XLSX library
Verify data accuracy: Compare row counts and sample values
Test error handling: Corrupted Excel file, Lambda timeout, /tmp cleanup
Use the Uploads page to test. Then Jobs to see the progress. And Data to see stats and import
 
Success Criteria

✅ Rust binary compiles successfully for Lambda (Amazon Linux 2)
✅ Lambda layer deployed and attached to fan-out function
✅ Excel → CSV conversion is 5-10x faster (15-30s → 2-3s)
✅ Lambda /tmp space managed correctly (512MB limit)
✅ Existing CSV uploads continue to work (zero regression)
✅ All workers unchanged (still download CSV chunks, no code changes)
✅ Memory usage reduced during Excel conversion phase
✅ Data accuracy 100% matches XLSX library output
✅ Lambda timeout sufficient (60-120s for large files)
✅ Chunking and worker processing logic completely unchanged
 

 LATER - Deploy Rust Binary as Lambda Layer (for production)
Cross-compile binary for Amazon Linux 2: cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
Create Lambda layer with compiled binary at /opt/bin/excel-converter
Upload layer to AWS (Lambda does NOT need Rust installed - just the binary)
Attach layer to fan-out Lambda function
Increase Lambda timeout to 60-120 seconds
Increase Lambda memory to 1-2GB

Why This Approach?

Simplicity: Only replacing the slow Excel reading in Lambda fan-out
Stability: Workers and all processing logic stay completely unchanged
Safety: Existing batching prevents DB flooding
Low Risk: Lambda is the only change point, clear rollback path

Tasks.title: Data Import POC Step 1 - Speed Up Column Mapping When Uploading A File For A Template
Tasks.description:
Problem
Browser parses 122MB Excel file for 16 seconds just to get column headers before upload.

Solution
Extract headers in the fan-out function (api.upload.fan-out.ts) during Excel → CSV conversion. Return headers immediately for column mapping.

Prerequisites

This requires Rust Excel converter to be set up first.
Use the Kroll import to create a staging table and template to be able to import to (AI should be able to handle this if you show it the file and ask it to create an in memory staging table will NVARCHAR Max)

Local Setup (Your Local Computer)
The API server runs on your local computer (not in Docker), so:
Install Rust on your local computer
Build Rust binary: cargo build --release
Place at project root: ./excel-converter

LATER - Production Setup (AWS Lambda)
Cross-compile Rust binary for Lambda (Amazon Linux 2)
Deploy compiled binary as Lambda layer at /opt/bin/excel-converter
Lambda does NOT need Rust installed - just runs the pre-compiled binary
 
Architecture

Current Flow:
Browser parses XLSB (16 sec) → Extract headers → Upload file → Fan-out → Workers

New Flow:
Upload file → Fan-out converts Excel to CSV → Extract headers (2 sec) → Return headers → User maps columns → Workers process

Key Insight: Fan-out already converts Excel → CSV. Extract headers during that conversion!
 
Key Points

Depends on Rust converter: Requires Rust Excel → CSV converter
Minimal change: Extract headers during existing Excel → CSV conversion in fan-out function
No extra conversion: Reuse the CSV that's already being created
Instant feedback: User sees headers in 2-3 seconds (not 16 seconds)
Works for all files: XLSX, XLSB, and CSV
Smart detection: Automatically detects if row 1 is headers or data
 
Detailed Flow

User uploads XLSB (122MB)
    ↓
Fan-out function receives file (api.upload.fan-out.ts)
    ↓
Convert Excel to CSV with Rust
    ↓
Read first 2 rows from CSV
    ↓
Detect if row 1 is headers:
  → Check if all strings, all unique, different from row 2
  → If yes: use row 1 as headers
  → If no: generate Column1, Column2, etc.
    ↓
Return response: { uploadId, headers, hasHeaders: true/false }
    ↓
Frontend receives headers immediately
    ↓
Call /api/templates/get-mappings with headers + templateId
    ↓
Display column mapping UI with suggested mappings
    ↓
User adjusts mappings if needed
    ↓
Continue with normal chunking/worker processing
 
Developer Tasks

1. Update Fan-Out Function to Extract Headers
File: app/routes/api.upload.fan-out.ts (runs locally as API route, deploys as Lambda)

During Excel → CSV conversion, read first 2 rows
Detect if row 1 is headers (all strings, all unique, different from row 2)
If no headers detected, use generic names: Column1, Column2, etc.
Return headers in fan-out response: { uploadId, headers, hasHeaders: true/false }
Continue with normal chunking

2. Create Column Mapping Endpoint
Create /api/templates/get-mappings endpoint
Accept { headers, templateId }
Return { mappings, templateColumns } using existing fuzzy matching logic

3. Update Frontend Upload
Remove client-side XLSX parsing (lines 70-86 in templates.$templateId.upload.tsx)
Receive headers from Lambda fan-out response
Call /api/templates/get-mappings with headers + templateId
Display column mapping UI with suggested mappings
If hasHeaders: false, show warning about generic column names

4. Test & Validate
Test XLSX file with headers → verify correct extraction
Test XLSB file (122MB Kroll) → verify fast (~2-3 sec), all 89 headers correct
Test CSV file → verify headers extracted
Test file without headers → verify generic names used
Test file with duplicate column names → verify fallback to generic names
Use Uploads page to test. Then Jobs to see progress. And Data to see stats
 
Success Criteria

✅ Header extraction takes 2-3 seconds (not 16 seconds)
✅ Headers returned in fan-out response
✅ Correctly detects if first row contains headers vs data
✅ Handles files without headers (generates generic column names)
✅ No client-side Excel parsing
✅ Works for XLSX, XLSB, and CSV files
✅ Column mapping UI shows immediately after upload
✅ Same code works locally (API route) and in production (Lambda)
 
Why This Approach?

Simplicity: Reuses existing fan-out Excel → CSV conversion
Performance: 8x faster than browser parsing (16s → 2-3s)
User Experience: Upload once, see headers immediately, map columns
Low Risk: No new functions, just extract headers during existing conversion
Portable: Same code runs locally and deploys as Lambda in production

As a Case Analyst, I want to be able to request a user to be added to a case
As a BART Admin, I want to add a user to a case

The user-request feature allows analysts to request that additional BART users be added to a specific case, while administrators manage and approve those requests. From within a case, analysts can open a modal showing eligible BART users not already assigned, select one or more, and submit the request. These pending users then appear in the admin view as grayed-out entries, where admins can approve or reject them; approval assigns the user to the case and updates the user list accordingly. An accompanying email workflow notifies the appropriate recipients when a new user request is submitted, indicating who was requested and for which case, with the potential to include a direct link. import { getDataSource } from "~/database/client";
import { CaseCreditor } from "~/database/entities/CaseCreditor";

export async function loader({ request }: Route.LoaderArgs): Promise<APIResponse> {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  const search = (url.searchParams.get("search") || "").trim().slice(0, 100);
  const limit = Math.min(parseInt(url.searchParams.get("limit") || "50", 10), 100);
  const offset = Math.max(parseInt(url.searchParams.get("offset") || "0", 10), 0);
  const caseId = "39C22B3B-5C1D-4BC5-8BE2-87E6BA780625"; // TODO: Get from session

  const db = await getDataSource();
  const repo = db.getRepository(CaseCreditor);

  const qb = repo
    .createQueryBuilder("c")
    // Join all related tables for searching
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.MMLStatus", "mml")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.CreditorSubType", "subType")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.CreditorRelationshipType", "relType")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.MailingStateProvince", "state")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.MailingCountry", "country")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.FDMType", "fdm")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.RelatedCaseCreditor", "related")
    .leftJoinAndSelect("c.CaseTaxForm", "taxForm")
    .where("c.CaseID = :caseId", { caseId })
    .andWhere("c.IsActive = :isActive", { isActive: true });

  if (search) {
    qb.andWhere(
      `(
        -- Direct columns
        c.Name LIKE :contains
        OR c.CMSID LIKE :prefix
        OR c.Email LIKE :contains
        OR c.AccountNumber LIKE :prefix
        OR c.FEIN = :exact
        OR c.InternalIdentifier LIKE :prefix
        OR c.PhoneNumber LIKE :contains
        OR c.FaxNumber LIKE :contains
        OR c.DebtorName LIKE :contains
        OR c.MailingAddress1 LIKE :contains
        OR c.MailingCity LIKE :contains
        OR c.MailingZip5 LIKE :prefix
        OR c.CreditorNote LIKE :contains
        -- FK lookups (search by name, not ID)
        OR mml.MMLStatus LIKE :contains
        OR subType.Name LIKE :contains
        OR relType.Name LIKE :contains
        OR state.Name LIKE :contains
        OR country.Country LIKE :contains
        OR fdm.Name LIKE :contains
        OR related.Name LIKE :contains
      )`,
      {
        contains: `%${search}%`,
        prefix: `${search}%`,
        exact: search
      }
    );
  }

  const [data, rowCount] = await qb
    .orderBy("c.Name", "ASC")
    .skip(offset)
    .take(limit)
    .getManyAndCount();

  return { data, rowCount };
}

import { useState } from "react";
import { useDebouncedValue } from "@mantine/hooks";

export default function Creditors() {
  const [searchValue, setSearchValue] = useState("");
  const [debouncedSearch] = useDebouncedValue(searchValue, 300);

  // Update InputText
  <InputText
    value={searchValue}
    onChange={(e) => setSearchValue(e.target.value)}
    placeholder="Search name, CMS ID, email..."
    // ...existing props
  />

  // Pass to grid

}

interface CreditorGridProps {
  search?: string;
}

export default function CreditorGrid({ search = "" }: CreditorGridProps) {
  const dataSource = useCallback(
    async (params: { startRow: number; endRow: number }) => {
      const { startRow, endRow } = params;
      const searchParam = search ? `&search=${encodeURIComponent(search)}` : "";

      const response = await fetch(
        `/api/creditors?limit=${endRow - startRow}&offset=${startRow}${searchParam}`
      );

      const result = await response.json();
      return { data: result.data, rowCount: result.rowCount };
    },
    [search] // Re-fetch when search changes
  );

  // ...rest of component
}

This document maps the groupings and columns defined in the XSD schemas for the Statement of Financial Affairs (SOFA) Form Crystal Reports, with database column mappings.
 
The x0020 in the XSD element names is XML encoding for a space character.
In XML/XSD, element names cannot contain spaces directly, so when these schemas are generated (typically from a data source like a
Crystal Reports dataset, SQL Server, or .NET DataSet), spaces in the original field names get encoded:

x0020 = space (hex 20 is the ASCII code for space)

Creating XSD schemas from DataSets

Tasks.title: Logic - Redaction Heirarchy
Tasks.description:
Consolidated Summary
Redaction for creditors follows a clear hierarchical precedence model. While redaction can be configured at multiple levels, the individual creditor level always takes precedence and overrides all others. Redaction must first be enabled at the case level, which acts as a global on/off switch for whether redaction is allowed within that case. Once enabled, the system evaluates redaction values in the following order of increasing priority: creditor type → creditor subtype → individual creditor. If a redaction is defined at the creditor type level, it applies to all creditors of that type unless overridden by a subtype-specific redaction. A creditor subtype redaction will override the type-level value when applicable. Finally, if a redaction is set directly on the individual creditor record, it will always supersede both type and subtype values and become the calculated redaction shown. When a creditor-level redaction is removed, the system should fall back to evaluating subtype and then type redactions in sequence. This hierarchy ensures flexibility while preserving explicit overrides at the most granular level.
 Clear Action Items
Confirm and document precedence logic
Case-level flag enables redaction globally.
Evaluation order: creditor type → creditor subtype → individual creditor.
Individual creditor redaction always wins.
Ensure write behavior at the creditor level
Writing a redaction directly to a creditor should always overwrite any existing calculated value, regardless of upstream configurations.
Implement fallback logic on removal
When a creditor-level redaction is removed, the system must re-evaluate subtype and then type redactions automatically.
Validate subtype override behavior
Confirm that subtype redactions reliably override type-level values when both exist.
Investigate inconsistent recalculation behavior
There appears to be a potential issue where updates at the creditor type level do not always recalculate as expected (possibly related to internal IDs). This should be reviewed and addressed.
Create a follow-up ticket
Track additional logic required for fallback and recalculation behavior, as this is part of broader case-level configuration and governance.
If you want, I can also convert this into a design doc section, engineering acceptance criteria, or ClickUp task description.
